title: Personal data; family background; parents and siblings
description: Isabel Miller fills out the personal data record with Irma Egland, covering her birth in Orofino in 1928, her maiden name Schlader, her mother who worked on the ranch and carried rural mail for 25 to 30 years, her farmer-rancher father George Schlader who died about 1962, and her two sisters and one brother.

title: Husband and children; education; jobs before marriage
description: Egland gives details about her husband Harry Egland Jr., a salesman in Moscow, their 1951 marriage, and their five children Nick, Mike, Hollis, Ed and Tony. She then describes graduating from the University of Idaho in 1950 and her hobbies of antiques, refinishing furniture, gardening and sewing.

title: Working through college; waitressing in Orofino; bank and odd jobs
description: Egland recounts working her way through college by waiting tables at a logging camp, lifeguarding, cleaning rat pens, and working as a bank teller in Orofino, Genesee and Moscow. She explains that in Orofino waitressing had more money and dignity than working in someone's house, unlike in the Genesee area.

title: Running the hay crew; cattle; division of farm labor
description: Egland describes running the family's hay crew, cooking and supervising the kids who work, driving truck but refusing tractors, and pitching bales until they grew too heavy at 60 to 70 pounds. With her husband working long hours at the tractor shop, the haying and the few beef cattle and one milk cow largely fall to her and the boys.

title: School board; girls' sports; clubs and 4-H
description: Egland talks about serving two years as the only woman on the Genesee school board, following a woman years earlier who was driven to resign, and how she speaks up for girls' sports such as track. She also mentions 13 years as a 4-H leader, Catholic Daughters, and the C.G. Club, a neighborhood women's group.

title: Rural versus urban life; childhood chores and schooling
description: Egland explains why she prefers country and small-town life, recalling her childhood envy of town girls as she walked two miles to school in long socks and rolled-up underwear. She describes how in her family boys and girls did the same chores, her brother could cook, and her parents worked together inside and out.

title: Siblings' education; calf herds; courtship and marriage
description: Egland tells how each child received a heifer calf at age ten and built a small herd to help fund college, and how her parents insisted she learn a skill even though she had no interest in college. She recounts meeting her husband at the University, courting three and a half years while he insisted she graduate first, and why the long courtship made for a better marriage; her family placed no pressure to marry, with unmarried aunts admired.

title: Children and childrearing; boys versus girls; mother's friendships
description: Egland discusses having five children who just came along, finding boys easier to raise than girls, her husband's wish for fewer, and solving childrearing problems on her own without advice or Dr. Spock. She also recalls her mother's friendship with an older neighbor and tensions over talk of war to raise meat prices before World War II.

title: Family recreation; ball games; reading and magazines
description: Egland describes the family's winter social life centered on high school ball games, which she attends because her husband insists, and their sons playing town-team basketball. In the evenings her husband reads on the davenport, the family reads a lot, watches little television, and takes the Moscow newspaper and a few magazines.

title: Television; rural life changes; marriage finances
description: Miller asks Egland about her television habits, leading to a discussion about how children today expect new cars compared to when Egland was young. Egland describes living four miles from Genesee and explains how she quit work upon marriage, helped buy a used car with her savings, and discusses her husband's transition from farming to other employment.

title: Church attendance; 4H activities; modern farming lifestyle
description: Egland mentions her husband does not attend church while the children participate in 4H at county fairs. She describes how modern farmers in the area work intensively in summer but take winters off to travel, contradicting traditional images of isolated farm life.

title: Food preservation; family decision making
description: Egland details her extensive canning practices using a pressure cooker, with help from her daughter Hollis but not her sons. She recounts how her husband Harry surprised her by purchasing their farm after they decided to move out of Genesee for the children's safety.

title: Life satisfaction; pressures on modern women
description: Egland expresses contentment with her life choices and argues that contemporary young women face excessive pressure to work and achieve compared to her generation. She states that her daughter Hollis should be free to choose either marriage or a career without societal pressure.
